name: Pantheon graded concrete dome
description: Rome’s Pantheon has a large concrete dome with lighter volcanic aggregate toward the crown, carried over a brick-faced concrete rotunda.

impact.note: One building in one city, a refinement of existing Roman concrete vaulting, studied and imitated by a few later dome builders.

date.label: Approximately 125–128 CE
date.basis: The cited source reports this approximate period or year; archaeological contexts date associated remains rather than a unique invention.

events.statement: The current Pantheon was completed in approximately 125–128 CE, with its graded concrete dome.

evidence.supports: The current Pantheon was completed in approximately 125–128 CE, with its graded concrete dome.
The source describes Roman builders of the Pantheon and this contribution.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest sourced date for the specific documented case; this does not establish invention or worldwide priority.

caveats: The exact building chronology and designer remain contested; a surviving dome does not prove global priority.

research.note: Independently inspected the cited Smarthistory article through the available indexed text and an accessible copy; its 125–128 completion date is an interpretation with debated chronology.

unresolved.note: A shared coarse-aggregate combination leaves the builders, carriers of know-how and source quarry for the Pantheon unconfirmed. Seek the 1930 Pantheon sample report, restoration records and a directly provenanced dome sample before assigning a quarry or transport route.

evidence.locator: pp. 708–710, Previous Studies and sample selection
evidence.supports: The first study of the Pantheon scoria used petrography; the later trace-element study did not analyse a Pantheon sample.

links.statement: Builders used yellow tuff and dark scoria as coarse aggregate to lighten the Pantheon’s crown. The Basilica Ulpia preserves the same combination in its earlier vault construction.
links.scope: Coarse volcanic aggregate in the Pantheon crown and the earlier Roman vaulting practice.
links.caveats: A finite-element model predicted lower peak hoop tension with graded densities. It compared whole-structure configurations, leaving the effect of the crown scoria alone unresolved. The route by which the builders acquired the technique remains unknown.

evidence.supports: The study provides sampled antecedents and identifies the same combination of yellow tuff and scoria in the Basilica Ulpia fragment and the Pantheon crown. Its discussion of Pantheon scoria draws on earlier restoration sampling.
The field study details the alternating coarse aggregate courses in the Basilica Ulpia fragment.

evidence.locator: pp. 26–29, models 5 and 6 and maximum-tension table
evidence.supports: The graded-density version produced lower peak hoop tension in the authors’ uncracked finite-element comparison. Their input on material grading came from De Fine Licht’s survey.
